title: US data centre additions return to growth in Q2 2026 as developers push construction and pipeline continues to expand
gist: Wood Mackenzie reports 54 GW of US data centre capacity added to the pipeline in Q2 2026 (up 29% y/y), taking the disclosed pipeline above 430 GW with ~80 GW under construction, while 400+ local moratoriums and power availability remain key constraints.

insights.claim: 54 GW of new data centre capacity entered the US pipeline in Q2 2026, up 29% year-over-year and 5% from Q1 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Pipeline additions are re-accelerating after a soft-looking Q1.

insights.claim: The cumulative disclosed US data centre pipeline exceeds 430 GW, with about 59% under active development.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Scale of announced load far exceeds what grids can deliver near term, so attrition is likely.

insights.claim: US data centre capacity under construction reached nearly 80 GW, up from 44 GW at the end of Q1 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Rapid shift from planning to construction supports demand for power equipment, construction and generation.

insights.claim: Q1 2026 US data centre additions were revised up to 52 GW from 36 GW because of disclosure lags, which Wood Mackenzie says does not alter the overall trend.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Early pipeline data understate additions; treat first prints as lower bounds.

insights.claim: PJM and ERCOT account for nearly half of all US data centre capacity under development, with PJM now ahead of ERCOT after about 20 GW entered active development in H1 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: PJM load growth is the biggest driver of capacity-price and supply-risk themes.

insights.claim: ERCOT has the most mature data centre pipeline, with over 40% of its development capacity already under construction.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Texas projects are nearest to energisation, but are exposed to the September 2026 permit pause.

insights.claim: The top five US data centre developers hold a quarter of planned and development capacity, and disclosed planned capex exceeds US$2.3 trillion.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Capex and capacity are concentrated in a few large players, simplifying exposure mapping for suppliers.

insights.claim: High-confidence utility data centre load commitments plateaued at about 300 GW in Q2 2026 as some utilities downgraded pipelines to remove speculative projects.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Utility-side filtering suggests speculative load is being weeded out; headline pipelines overstate real demand.

insights.claim: Committed US data centre capacity with signed electricity service or construction agreements grew to 201 GW, showing projects moving from advanced discussions to signed agreements.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Contracted load is the harder demand signal for generation and grid investment.

insights.claim: PJM is the market most exposed to supply risk, with Wood Mackenzie's risked supply view through 2036 falling short of high-confidence load commitments.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Supports upward pressure on PJM power and capacity prices and demand for new generation.

insights.claim: More than 400 US data centre moratoriums have been enacted since January 2026, affecting 18% of tracked sites and more than 100 GW of planned capacity, versus only 45 such actions across 2023-2025.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Local opposition is now a material gating factor on siting and timelines.

insights.claim: A September 2026 pause on new data centre permits in Texas, with an audit of the existing pipeline, puts more than 60 GW of tracked planned projects under scrutiny.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch Texas outcomes for ERCOT load forecasts and developer timelines.

insights.claim: 92% of data centre moratoriums target land use or zoning approvals and last six to twelve months on average, suggesting lawmakers want time to build frameworks rather than impose outright bans.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Moratoriums look like delays rather than cancellations, limiting long-run demand damage.
insights.quote: the current moratoriums suggest that lawmakers are seeking time to develop stronger frameworks rather than moving to impose outright bans

insights.claim: Power availability and local opposition will remain the key constraints on near-term US data centre buildout.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Power-secured and well-permitted sites carry a premium; monitor interconnection and community risk.
